title: Longest Reading Streak
story: A reading app numbers days from launch: day 0 is launch day, day 1 the next, and early testers have negative days. Each time you read, it logs the day number. The log syncs from your phone and tablet, so it arrives jumbled, and a day you read twice appears twice.
The app shows your best streak: the longest run of back-to-back days with at least one read.
task: Write longestStreak(days). Return the length of the longest run of consecutive whole numbers d, d + 1, ..., d + L - 1 that all appear in days. Repeated day numbers count once.
An empty log returns 0. Aim for O(n) time; sorting works but costs O(n log n).

examples.explanation: Days 10, 11, 12, 13 make a streak of 4; days 3, 4, 5 a streak of 3. Day 11 appears twice but is one day, so the answer is 4, not 5.
Days -2, -1, 0, 1 make a streak of 4 across launch day. Day 7 stands alone.
No reading, so the best streak is 0.

hints: In the first example, which days could be the first day of a streak? What is true about the day before each?
Day d starts a streak exactly when d - 1 is not in the log. Days 3 and 10 start streaks; 4, 5, 11, 12 and 13 do not.
From each starting day you could count upward until the streak breaks, if you could ask "is this day in the log?" in one step. Which structure does that, and also removes duplicates?

Put every day in a hash set. For each day d in the set, skip it if d - 1 is also there. Otherwise count d, d + 1, d + 2, ... while present, and keep the longest. Counting only from streak starts touches each day once.
bruteForce: For each day, count upward, scanning the log to check whether d + 1, d + 2 and so on appear.

Each check scans n entries, and a long streak is recounted from every one of its days: O(n³) in the worst case, hopeless for 100,000 entries. Even with a set, starting from every day recounts a streak of length L about L²/2 times: one 100,000-day streak costs 5 billion steps.

js: * @param {number[]} days  day numbers, in any order, repeats allowed
* @return {number} length of the longest run of consecutive days

tests.note: repeat inside a streak must not break it: defeats a sort-and-scan that resets on equal neighbours
repeats must not lengthen a streak: defeats a sort-and-scan that counts equal neighbours
extreme values: no array indexed by day
one streak of 10 with repeats, unsorted

js: const logged = new Set(days); // also drops repeated days
if (logged.has(d - 1)) continue; // not the first day of a streak
py: logged = set(days)  # also drops repeated days
if d - 1 in logged:  # not the first day of a streak
walkthrough: Two ideas fit together. A hash set answers "did I read on day x?" in one step and drops repeats. And you only count a streak from its first day, the one whose previous day is missing, so each streak is walked once.
• 12: 11 is in the set, so 12 is mid-streak. Skip.
• 10: 9 is missing, so 10 starts a streak. Count 11, 12, 13, then 14 is missing. Length 4. best = 4.
• 5, 11 and 13: each has its previous day in the set. Skip.
• 3: 2 is missing, so count 4, 5, then 6 is missing. Length 3. best stays 4.

The loop inside a loop is still O(n): the inner while only runs from streak starts, and each day belongs to one streak, so it steps over each day once overall. Loop over the set, not the original list, or a repeated starting day would recount its streak.
solution.timeWhy: Building the set is O(n), and each day is visited once by the outer loop and at most once by an inner count.
solution.spaceWhy: The set holds every distinct day.
solution.takeaway: A hash set gives O(1) membership tests. Combine it with "only start from the beginning of a run" (the previous element is missing) and nested-looking loops become linear.
